title: AI Glossary
source: Terms and scope follow https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-definitions; definitions rewritten in own words

terms.definition: Someone secretly tampers with how a model is trained or copied, so the resulting model carries hidden flaws or behaviors the attacker wants.
A hypothetical system that can learn and reason across almost any task at or above human level, instead of being good at one narrow job.
AI that works more like an agent than a chatbot. It takes a goal, plans the steps, uses tools such as a browser or code runner, checks the results and adjusts until the task is done.
The work of making an AI system's goals and behavior match what people actually intend and value.
Standard tests used to score and compare models on things like question answering, image recognition, coding or following instructions.
Being able to work with AI well and responsibly. You know what it can and can't do, you check its output instead of trusting it blindly, and you keep up as the tools change.
The field concerned with keeping AI systems reliable and harmless, including when they are very capable, used by millions, or pushed into situations nobody planned for.
All the layers needed to build and run AI, from hardware and computing power up through data, models and the software people actually use.
The full path of an AI project, from gathering and preparing data to training, testing, deploying and then making predictions in real use. Each stage depends on the one before it.
A fixed series of steps for solving a problem, a bit like following a recipe.
What happens when many organizations rely on the same or nearly the same models, algorithms or data, so they all make the same mistakes together.
A group of AI systems that share information and coordinate so they behave like one connected unit.
Building machines that do things we'd call intelligent. John McCarthy, Stanford's first AI faculty member, coined the term in 1955.
A part of a neural network that lets the model weigh which pieces of the input matter most for the output it is producing.
Technology carrying out a task exactly as a person specified it. The human sets the rules, the machine follows them.
The way a neural network learns from errors. It traces the mistake backward through the layers to see which connections caused it, then corrects them.
A diagram of variables linked by probabilities, showing how one factor influences another.
When an AI system gives results that systematically favor or disadvantage certain groups of people.
Datasets so large that ordinary tools can't handle them, but AI can dig through them to find patterns.
A program that holds a conversation with a person through text or voice.
Software whose code is kept private, so outsiders can't read, change or reuse it. Also called proprietary software.
The area of AI that lets computers make sense of images and video, much like human eyesight does.
How much input, such as text, a model can take in and keep track of at once.
Training a model by showing it pairs of similar and different examples so it learns what makes things alike or unlike.
Stretching a training set by making altered copies of the data you already have, such as flipping or cropping images, instead of collecting new data.
Searching big datasets with statistics and machine learning to find patterns and trends.
An attack where someone slips bad, changed or wrongly labeled examples into training data to damage what the model learns.
A model that reaches a prediction by asking a chain of yes/no questions about the data, splitting at each step until it lands on an answer.
Machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers to pick up complicated patterns on their own.
A generative model that creates things like images by learning to add noise to data and then remove it step by step.
Cutting down the number of variables in a dataset while keeping the information that matters most.
Lists of numbers that stand in for words, images or other items, built so that similar things end up with similar numbers.
Combining several models, often weak ones, so their joint prediction is more accurate and steadier than any single model.
Designing and using AI in line with human values, with attention to fairness, transparency and the wider good of society.
An older style of AI that copies how a specialist decides things, using stored facts and if-then rules.
Techniques that make a model's decisions understandable to people, so it isn't a sealed black box.
Training one model across many devices or servers, each keeping its own data locally so the raw data never gets sent anywhere.
Getting a model to handle a new task from just a handful of examples.
Taking a model that is already trained and training it a bit more on data from a specific task or field.
A very large model, usually a transformer, trained on broad data and then adapted for many different uses.
A general-purpose model at or close to the most capable level currently available.
AI that produces new content, such as text, images, music, code or video.
Two neural networks pitted against each other. One generates fake samples, the other tries to spot them, and the contest pushes the fakes toward looking real.
A family of large language models built on the transformer design that write human-like text from a prompt.
A chip first built for rendering graphics that can run huge numbers of calculations in parallel, which is why it suits AI training.
When a model states something false, misleading or made up as if it were fact.
An approach that keeps people's needs, values and wellbeing at the center while AI is built and rolled out.
The study of how people use and interact with computer systems.
A setup where a person gives feedback or can step in as part of how the AI system runs.
A setting chosen before training starts, instead of being learned from the data.
A giant tech company with enormous data center networks that can quickly scale up computing, storage and cloud services on demand.
When a trained model is put to use and makes predictions or decisions on data it hasn't seen before.
How well a person can follow the reasoning behind a model's output.
A simple method for classification and regression that looks at the closest known examples and goes with what they say.
A structured store of information laid out as things and the relationships connecting them.
A model trained on huge amounts of text so it can understand and produce natural language.
A compressed, abstract space where complex data like images or text is encoded in fewer dimensions while keeping its key features.
The practice of running LLM-based applications in production, covering the whole lifecycle from deployment to upkeep.
A formula that scores how far off a model's predictions are from the correct answers. Also called a cost or objective function.
A branch of AI where computers find patterns in data and make decisions from them, rather than following hand-written rules.
A model of a sequence of events where the next step depends only on the current state, not on how things got there.
Practices that mix machine learning, software engineering and DevOps to deploy, monitor and maintain models reliably in production.
A simplified mathematical version of some real-world process or relationship, used to predict outcomes or understand patterns.
A model getting worse over time because real-world data has shifted away from what it was trained on.
AI that can handle several kinds of data together, such as text, images, audio and video.
The part of AI about getting computers to understand, interpret and produce human language.
A model loosely based on the brain, made of layers of connected artificial neurons that pass information along.
Software whose design is made freely available for anyone to look at and use.
An AI model released with its weights, code, training data (or a thorough, checkable account of it) and tools, so others can run, inspect, reproduce, change and improve it.
An AI model whose main components, mainly the trained weights, are published so anyone can download it.
The method a model uses to adjust its settings step by step so it makes fewer errors.
When a model memorizes its training data too closely, including the noise and flukes, and then does poorly on new data.
An internal value of a model that gets learned and adjusted during training.
Using data, statistics and machine learning to forecast what is likely to happen next.
Writing and refining instructions so a language model gives the kind of output you want.
A security attack where crafted input tricks a language model into doing something it wasn't meant to do.
Letting a language model look up outside, current information first so its answer is better grounded.
An AI system built for hard problems that works through them in a logical, step-by-step chain of thought.
Learning by trial and error, where an agent tries actions in an environment and improves from the results.
The frameworks, principles and practices for building and using AI ethically and safely.
The field combining engineering and computer science, and increasingly AI, to build machines that carry out physical tasks.
Predictable relationships showing that model performance improves as model size, training data and computing power go up.
A model teaches itself by making up puzzles from raw data, like hiding part of an input, and then solving them.
Working out the meaning of language by looking at how words, phrases and symbols relate to each other.
Understanding and reasoning about the 3D physical world, including where things are, how they move and how they affect each other.
Training on labeled data, where every input example comes with its correct answer.
Data produced by algorithms or simulations instead of being collected from real events.
A container for numbers arranged in any number of dimensions, like a spreadsheet extended into more directions.
Splitting text into small pieces called tokens, which can be words, word fragments or single characters, so a language model can process it.
Earlier AI that ran on hand-coded rules, logic and human-defined knowledge instead of learning from data.
The examples, such as text, images or audio, used to teach a model a task.
Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for a related one.
A neural network design that uses attention to look at all parts of the input at the same time instead of one piece after another. It changed the direction of modern AI.
Alan Turing's 1950 idea for judging whether a machine can behave so much like a person that you can't tell the difference.
Training on data with no labels or preset categories, so the model has to find structure by itself.
A database built to store and quickly search the number-vector versions of text, images or audio.
The transformer design, first made for language, adapted to analyze images.
The numbers inside a neural network that set how strongly neurons connect, and so shape how the model handles information.
A model doing a task or recognizing a category it was never specifically trained on, using only its general knowledge.
